verification: Every PMID resolved through NCBI E-utilities esummary (title, first author, journal, year compared) and abstracts read through efetch; full text read through Europe PMC where open access (Wang & Dreesen 2018, PMC6115505). The Hormone Cell Atlas portal was fetched live (HTTP 200) and its About/FAQ text read; the Science full text and supplement returned HTTP 403, so only abstract- and portal-level facts are taught. ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API searched for senolytic skin-ageing trials (none). Nothing is included on the strength of a guide reference alone.
grader: Graded 2026-09-24 by the agent under Omar Saleem's delegation ("you should be able to do that from the guide"); rule set below; final review Dr. Hannah-Shmouni
gradingRule: Grade = certainty the source gives for the specific clinical statement the lesson makes, on the guides' A–D scale. A: consistent large RCTs or approval-grade evidence. B: at least one well-designed, adequately powered RCT or an independent, quality-stratified meta-analysis (either direction). C: small or sponsor-funded RCTs without independent replication, or pooled trials dominated by them. D: animal, in-vitro, mechanistic, case series, manufacturer dossiers. 'context' = history, reviews used for framing, trial registrations without results, analytical or regulatory records (regulatory records are primary for status statements, not graded for efficacy). Where the two guides disagree, the lesson states both and the claim takes the grade the primary evidence supports. Observational studies (added 2026-09-24, GRADE starting point, for the final reviewer to confirm): adequately sized cohort, case-control or cross-sectional studies grade C for the association they measured; small or single-centre ones grade D; any causal claim drawn from observational data grades D. Meta-analyses of observational studies grade at most B, and only for association. Guidelines and consensus statements are 'context', cited for what they recommend, not graded as evidence.

claims.text: The skin works as a peripheral neuro-immuno-endocrine organ: reviews describe four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) whose cells make and respond to hormones and signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the circulation. This is a mechanistic framework drawn from cell, tissue and animal work.
claims.reviewNote: the guide's ch.6 framing, checked against its own references
claims.gradeDecision: D — mechanism reviews; taught as framework

claims.text: Skin cells carry the enzymes to make steroids from cholesterol (CYP11A1) and to activate circulating precursors (11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, aromatase), producing cortisol, DHT and estradiol locally; this rests mainly on cell, tissue and biochemical studies.
claims.reviewNote: the guide itself calls this literature 'mechanistic … not a dosing rationale'

claims.text: Human scalp hair follicles kept in organ culture respond to CRH by making POMC products, secrete cortisol, and switch off their own CRH in response to glucocorticoid — an HPA-like loop running without systemic connections (human tissue, ex vivo).
claims.reviewNote: stated as ex vivo

claims.text: In mice, deleting glucocorticoid synthesis in keratinocytes causes spontaneous skin inflammation and worse experimental dermatitis: keratinocyte-made glucocorticoids set local immune tone (animal evidence, with a human association with inflammatory skin disease).
claims.reviewNote: species now labelled; the guide omits it

claims.text: The skin also runs shortened thyroid-like (TRH, TSH, deiodinase-generated T3) and somatotropic (GH/IGF-1) loops; the thyroid-like evidence comes mainly from mouse models and the follicle GH/IGF-1 loop from human follicles ex vivo.
claims.reviewNote: evidence type named per loop

claims.text: The skin supplies a whole-body hormone system: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3 in human skin, and vitamin D3 is carried into the circulation to be hydroxylated to 25(OH)D and then calcitriol (skin-to-body signalling).
claims.reviewNote: uncontested
claims.gradeDecision: established human physiology — not graded on the intervention scale

claims.text: Reviews describe a skin contribution to circulating androgens and estrogens, especially in older people — a second skin-to-body route, supported mainly by biochemical data.
claims.reviewNote: worded as 'reviews describe'

claims.text: Systemic hormones act on skin (body-to-skin): cortisol excess thins the dermis and causes striae and bruising; hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse skin and myxoedema. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen and lists suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes) and rapidly progressive virilisation among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology.
claims.reviewNote: the referral list is reported as the guide's recommendation

claims.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas (Science 2026) analysed RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them, and mapped putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types.
claims.reviewNote: abstract- and portal-level facts only; the guide's 74%/93% figures are not taught
claims.gradeDecision: D — transcriptomic; primary for what was measured

claims.text: The atlas's authors describe its scores as putative and hypothesis-generating, not functional hormones and receptors, and leave validation to in vitro and in vivo work; more generally, transcript levels alone often fail to predict protein levels. A transcriptomic map therefore shows capacity, not secretion or effect.
claims.reviewNote: matches the guide's own caveat ('a map to confirm, not proof of secretion')
claims.gradeDecision: context — the resource's own statement plus methods review

claims.text: The guide infers from the atlas that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signalling networks — an inference from transcriptomic prediction, not a measurement.
claims.reviewNote: the guide labels it as inference; the course keeps that label

claims.text: Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and local steroid-metabolising enzymes modify potency, so the cutaneous response need not mirror the dose; receptor presence is a hypothesis-generating starting point that needs validation, and says nothing yet about efficacy in people.
claims.reviewNote: no product is named

claims.text: The guide's testing pearl says serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls with sunscreen use; an independent systematic review found that sunscreen blocks vitamin D synthesis under artificial UV, but randomized field trials of daily moderate-SPF sunscreen did not lower 25(OH)D, and high-SPF products have not been trialled.
claims.reviewNote: teach the evidence; finding sent to the author
claims.gradeDecision: C — independent review of small field trials; the guide's pearl is not supported as worded

claims.text: Senescent cells are permanently growth-arrested yet still secreting; the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (IL-6, IL-8, matrix metalloproteinases, growth factors) was characterised in cultured human cells after DNA damage.
claims.reviewNote: register labelled

claims.text: In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a are more numerous with age in both epidermis and dermis; no single universal marker identifies senescent cells, so counts depend on the marker used.
claims.reviewNote: uncontested

claims.text: In 178 adults of the Leiden Longevity Study, more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin were associated with ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and higher perceived age independent of chronological age; people in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked about 3 years younger than those in the highest. This is an association, not evidence of cause.
claims.reviewNote: industry co-author disclosed

claims.text: Skin collagen falls with age; aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1, fragmented collagen and fibroblasts under less mechanical tension that make less procollagen, and culture work shows fragmentation feeds back to raise MMP-1. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible but not shown.
claims.reviewNote: the guide's 'SASP-driven MMPs degrade dermal collagen' softened to plausible

claims.text: Causal evidence that senescent cells drive ageing comes from mice: clearing p16-positive cells extended healthy lifespan and senolytics improved function and survival in old mice; skin was checked only for safety (thickness, fibrosis, wound closure), and clearing p16-positive cells during healing slowed wound closure.
claims.reviewNote: species labelled

claims.text: Human senotherapy data are small pilots with tissue-marker endpoints — an open-label senolytic pilot in 9 patients reduced epidermal p16/p21-positive cells; an exploratory topical rapamycin RCT (36 enrolled, 19 lost) reduced skin p16 — clinical improvement in that trial was described only in 'multiple participants', and no adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found on PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov (checked 24 September 2026). The guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.
claims.reviewNote: the guide's C-versus-D inconsistency noted in findings
claims.gradeDecision: C/D — pilots; absence of outcome trials stated as a dated search result

claims.text: Interventions on the ageing matrix with human trials: daily sunscreen slowed photoageing in a 903-person community RCT (B); topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials and the guide rates topical retinoids first-line GRADE A; topical retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small RCT (C), and within a week lowered MMPs and raised collagen synthesis in aged human skin.
claims.reviewNote: no concentrations or regimens taught

authorFindings: A&RE ch.7 ref 1 — the Hormone Cell Atlas is now in print: Fei L, Huang-Doran I, et al. Science 2026;393(6806):eaeb2672 (2 Jul 2026), PMID 42207862. The guide's 'published online May 28, 2026' matches the PubMed entry date.

A&RE ch.7 — the figures '~74% of cell types predicted to produce, and 93% to respond to, at least one hormone' and 'endocrine identity tracks cellular lineage more than tissue of origin' could not be verified from the abstract, the atlas portal or press coverage (full text and supplement paywalled). The course teaches only the abstract- and portal-level facts (379 genes, ~14 million cells and nuclei, 47 tissues). Please confirm these against the paper's text.

A&RE ch.7 testing pearl — 'serum 25-OH vitamin D … falls with low UVB exposure and sunscreen use regardless of oral intake': Neale et al. 2019 (Br J Dermatol, systematic review) found little evidence that real-life sunscreen use lowers 25(OH)D (the two randomized field trials, SPF ~16, showed no effect; high-SPF products untested), and dietary or supplemental vitamin D is itself converted to 25(OH)D (Bikle 2014), so 'regardless of oral intake' does not hold. The course teaches the trial evidence and keeps sun-protection advice unchanged.

A&RE ch.7 senescence paragraph — 'blunting neighboring cells' responsiveness to estrogen, IGF-1, and retinoids, while estrogen loss at menopause is itself associated with a heavier senescent burden and slower fibroblast turnover [4,6]' and 'correcting a true deficiency works partly by easing the senescent … state': neither cited source addresses this (Slominski & Wortsman 2000; Wang & Dreesen 2018, full text read), and a targeted PubMed search found no human study. The course does not teach these statements.

A&RE ch.7 — 'SASP-driven MMPs degrade dermal collagen' is stated as established. The human evidence is that aged dermis has more fibroblast MMP-1 and fragmented collagen (Fisher 2009; Varani 2006) and that senescent cells secrete MMPs in culture (Coppé 2008); that senescent cells are the main source in living skin is plausible, not shown. Suggest 'are thought to'.

A&RE ch.17 internal inconsistency — the text and table grade senolytics' human evidence GRADE C, while the 'three things to remember' strip says senolytics have 'no human outcome data (D)'. The underlying studies (open-label pilots of 9 and 14 patients, biomarker endpoints) fit D for any clinical claim; the course says so and adds that no adequately sized trial with skin-ageing outcomes was found (September 2026); the one exploratory topical-rapamycin RCT described clinical change only qualitatively.

A&RE ch.6 — 'Independent work shows keratinocyte-derived, de novo glucocorticoids actively police local immune tone' (Phan 2021): the functional evidence is from mice (keratinocyte Cyp11b1 deletion). Worth naming the species, as the chapter does elsewhere ('cell and ex-vivo').

A&RE ch.5 — 'reduces collagen by roughly 1% per year' (ref 1, Shuster 1975): the abstract confirms that skin collagen falls with age and is lower in women but gives no annual rate, and the full text was not accessible. The course does not quote the 1% figure; please confirm the source of the rate.

A&RE ch.5 — 'retinoids … remain first-line GRADE A' carries no citation. Suggested primary: Sitohang et al. 2022 (systematic review of 7 RCTs of topical tretinoin for photoageing, PMID 35620028); for naturally aged skin, Kafi et al. 2007 (RCT, PMID 17515510).

Not in either guide, worth adding — Ressler 2006 and Waaijer 2016 (senescent cells in human skin, and their link with wrinkles and perceived age), Fisher 2009 and Varani 2006 (the MMP-1–collagen fragmentation loop in aged human dermis), Coppé 2008 (the SASP primary), Chung 2019 (the one randomized human-skin senomorphic study), Hughes 2013 (sunscreen RCT, photoageing), Neale 2019 (sunscreen and vitamin D), and the atlas portal's own statement that its predictions are 'putative and hypothesis-generating'.

Baker 2016 (2026-09-24, from the claim-support full-text read): clearing p16-positive cells during wound healing slowed wound closure in mice (Extended Data Fig. 10), consistent with transient senescence aiding repair (Haykal 2026). This is worth a line in A&RE ch.13/17, where senolytics are discussed for skin.
